Linear-Readout Floors and Threshold Recovery in Computation in Superposition

Hector Borobia Email: hecboar@doctor.upv.es Note: Corresponding author. Affiliation: VRAIN – Valencian Research Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain    Elies Seguí-Mas Affiliation: Department of Economics and Social Sciences, Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain    Guillermina Tormo-Carbó Affiliation: Department of Business Organisation, Universitat Politècnica de València, Valencia, Spain
Abstract

Two recent approaches to computation in superposition reach different recursive capacity regimes: Hänni et al. certify O~​(d3/2)\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2}) computable features in width dd via an approximate-linear recursive template, while Adler and Shavit reach near-quadratic capacity (up to logarithmic factors) using thresholded Boolean recovery. The main contribution of this paper is conceptual: we argue these results are not contradictory because they maintain different interface invariants, and we formalize the distinction.

As a tool, we record a rank–trace Welch-type lower bound for biorthogonal linear readouts: for F≫dF\gg d, the worst-case off-diagonal cross-talk of any unit-diagonal linear readout is Ω(d−1/2)\Omega(d^{-1/2}), and the bound is tight on average for unit-norm tight frames. At quadratic feature load F=d2F=d^{2}, random-support threshold recovery succeeds for sparsities s=O⁡(d/log⁡d)s=O(d/\log d), while linear readouts still incur Ω⁡(s/d)\Omega(s/d) average per-coordinate squared error on Bernoulli sparse states. Matching the Welch floor against the published tolerance of the Hänni correction layer explains the d3/2d^{3/2} scale as a compatibility threshold for that template, not a universal upper bound. Robust nonlinear reset beyond the Hänni template is left open.

Keywords: 
computation in superposition , sparse autoencoders , mechanistic interpretability , neural network capacity , Boolean circuits , Welch bound

1 Introduction

Superposition—the hypothesis that neural networks represent more conceptual features than they have neurons—has become a central concept in mechanistic interpretability [5, 3, 16]. With worst-case coherence on the order of d−1/2d^{-1/2}, a width-dd network can support a quadratic-scale packing of directions, while weaker passive-representation notions such as Johnson–Lindenstrauss embeddings allow much larger state sets. The question of how many features can be actively computed with, rather than merely stored or passively embedded, is substantially more subtle.

Two recent papers have attacked this question from different angles and arrived at results that, on their face, appear contradictory:

  1. 1.

    Hänni et al. [7] show that a network of width dd can recursively emulate any ss-sparse Boolean circuit of width m=O~​(d3/2)m=\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2}) and polynomial depth, by alternating one-step universal-AND (U-AND) computation layers with error-correction layers. This suggests a recursive capacity exponent of αH=3/2\alpha_{H}=3/2.

  2. 2.

    Adler and Shavit [1] prove parameter-description lower bounds for recursive pairwise-AND (2-AND) computation and give nearly matching constructive algorithms. In the square-matrix network model with Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) parameters and O⁡(1)O(1) average description length per parameter, their lower bound implies that computing m′m^{\prime} 2-AND outputs requires Ω⁡(m′​log⁡m′)\Omega(\sqrt{m^{\prime}\log m^{\prime}}) neurons, while their construction uses O⁡(m′​log⁡m′)O(\sqrt{m^{\prime}}\log m^{\prime}) neurons. Inverting gives capacity between Ω⁡(n2/log2⁡n)\Omega(n^{2}/\log^{2}n) and O⁡(n2/log⁡n)O(n^{2}/\log n), suggesting αA​S=2\alpha_{AS}=2 up to logarithmic factors.

The gap between d3/2d^{3/2} and d2d^{2} spans a factor of Θ⁡(d1/2)\Theta(d^{1/2}), which for realistic model widths (d≈1000d\approx 1000–40004000) corresponds to 30×30\times–60×60\times more computable features.

Contributions

We make the following contributions.

  1. 1.

    We separate two interface invariants used in recent work: approximate ε\varepsilon-linear decodability in the recursive construction of Hänni et al., and thresholded Boolean recovery in Adler–Shavit.

  2. 2.

    We prove a Biorthogonal Welch Floor (Theorem 7.1). For any code Ψ∈ℝd×F\Psi\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times F} and linear readout G∈ℝF×dG\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times d} with unit diagonal (G​Ψ)i​i=1(G\Psi)_{ii}=1, the off-diagonal cross-talk obeys

    1F⁡(F−1)​∑i≠j|(G​Ψ)i​j|2≥F−dd⁡(F−1)\frac{1}{F(F-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}|(G\Psi)_{ij}|^{2}\geq\frac{F-d}{d(F-1)}

    whenever F>dF>d. In particular, if F≫dF\gg d, some off-diagonal cross-talk is Ω(d−1/2)\Omega(d^{-1/2}).

  3. 3.

    We show that the Welch floor is tight at the level of average squared cross-talk for unit-norm tight frames (Proposition 7.2). Thus the bound is not merely an artifact of the rank–trace proof.

  4. 4.

    We prove a coherence-based threshold recovery lemma (Theorem 7.6). If a unit-norm code has coherence μ\mu, then every ss-sparse Boolean state can be exactly recovered by thresholding Φ⊤​x\Phi^{\top}x whenever aggregate interference plus score noise satisfies s​μ+ν<1/2s\mu+\nu<1/2.

  5. 5.

    We specialize this lemma to random codes (Corollary 7.7). For F=d2F=d^{2} random unit vectors, the coherence is O⁡(log⁡d/d)O(\sqrt{\log d/d}) with high probability, so constant-sparsity threshold recovery is compatible with quadratic feature load. This illustrates why thresholded recovery does not contradict the Welch floor.

  6. 6.

    We prove an average linear-energy lower bound for random sparse states (Theorem 8.1). Under any unit-diagonal rank-dd linear readout interface, Bernoulli sparse states of expected sparsity ss incur average per-coordinate squared linear readout error Ω⁡(s/d)\Omega(s/d) when F≫dF\gg d.

  7. 7.

    We prove a random-support threshold recovery theorem (Theorem 8.3). For random unit-vector codes, threshold recovery succeeds with high probability whenever

    ‖Φ⊤​η‖∞+C​s​log⁡(F/δ)d<12.\|\Phi^{\top}\eta\|_{\infty}+C\sqrt{\frac{s\log(F/\delta)}{d}}<\frac{1}{2}.

    At quadratic feature load F=d2F=d^{2}, this gives noiseless recovery for random supports of size s=O⁡(d/log⁡d)s=O(d/\log d) (Corollary 8.4).

  8. 8.

    We explicitly frame this as a distributional separation between different interface criteria: linear readout error and threshold success. The result is not uniform over all supports, does not construct a recursive reset module, and does not imply a universal recursive capacity theorem.

  9. 9.

    We show that matching the unavoidable d−1/2d^{-1/2} linear cross-talk scale to the tolerance of the published Hänni correction layer gives a d3/2d^{3/2} compatibility threshold for that template. This is not claimed as a universal upper bound for all ε\varepsilon-linear or nonlinear recursive computation.

  10. 10.

    We restate the Adler–Shavit comparison with the logarithmic gap explicit:

    Ω⁡(n2/log2⁡n)≤FrecAS​(n)≤O⁡(n2/log⁡n),\Omega(n^{2}/\log^{2}n)\leq F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(n)\leq O(n^{2}/\log n),

    under their parameter-description and network-size assumptions.

  11. 11.

    We formulate robust nonlinear threshold reset beyond the Hänni template as an open problem. For γ>0\gamma>0, such a reset is explicitly not an ε\varepsilon-linear reset with output error o(d−1/2)o(d^{-1/2}); it must use nonlinear or thresholded recovery.

  12. 12.

    We treat SAE observations as motivation and possible empirical context, not as evidence for the mathematical capacity bounds.

2 Background

2.1 Computation in Superposition

Let a neural network have hidden dimension dd (number of neurons). We say it represents m≫dm\gg d features in superposition if its activation vector a→​(x)∈ℝd\vec{a}(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} can be written approximately as Φ​𝐛\Phi\mathbf{b} where Φ∈ℝd×m\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} is a feature-encoding matrix and 𝐛∈{0,1}m\mathbf{b}\in\{0,1\}^{m} is a sparse Boolean vector with ‖𝐛‖1≤s\left\lVert\mathbf{b}\right\rVert_{1}\leq s.

Definition 2.1 (ε\varepsilon-linear representation [7]).

Features f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m} are ε\varepsilon-linearly represented by activations a→:X→ℝd\vec{a}:X\to\mathbb{R}^{d} if there exists a readout matrix 𝐑∈ℝm×d\mathbf{R}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} such that |r→k⋅a→​(x)−fk​(x)|<ε|\vec{r}_{k}\cdot\vec{a}(x)-f_{k}(x)|<\varepsilon for all k∈{1,…,m}k\in\{1,\ldots,m\} and x∈Xx\in X.

2.2 The Universal AND Circuit and Error Correction

The key primitive studied by Hänni et al. is the universal AND (U-AND) circuit. Their Theorem 14/Corollary 15 shows that a single-layer MLP of width dd can ε\varepsilon-linearly represent the U-AND on ss-sparse inputs with one-step capacity O~​(d2)\widetilde{O}(d^{2}). The d3/2d^{3/2} scale appears in the published recursive proof certificate, because the computation-layer error estimate must fit within the tolerance of the subsequent error-correction layer (Theorem 21 therein).

Adler and Shavit [1] escape this bottleneck by employing explicit thresholding at 1/21/2 with a constant Boolean margin of 1/41/4, removing error accumulation entirely.

2.3 Recent Related Work

Several concurrent works inform our analysis. Ivanov et al. [8] develop a spectral theory of superposition in which capacity-saturated toy models exhibit tight-frame-like structure. This provides related geometric context for Welch-type arguments, although our theorem does not assume that trained models are in this regime. Sarkar and Deka [14] derive a compressed-sensing capacity function g⁡(α)=1/((1−α)​ln⁡(1/(1−α)))g(\alpha)=1/((1{-}\alpha)\ln(1/(1{-}\alpha))) for knowledge distillation, providing a storage bound that we place in our reference-scale comparison alongside the computation bounds of Hänni and Adler–Shavit. Liu et al. [11] connect the superposition regime to neural scaling laws, motivating our Prediction A. Michaud et al. [12] show that feature manifolds can make SAEs learn fewer features than latents, partially explaining why observed dictionary sizes fall far below theoretical bounds. Prieto et al. [13] demonstrate that feature correlations can make interference constructive rather than purely destructive, suggesting that worst-case linear-interface analyses may be pessimistic for structured data, motivating Prediction A.2.

The threshold-recovery result used below is a standard coherence-based support-recovery argument, closely related to sparse recovery in compressed sensing. We include it not as a new sparse recovery theorem, but to make explicit the interface distinction between small-error linear readout and thresholded Boolean recovery: the former is constrained by a Welch-type worst-case cross-talk floor, whereas the latter only requires sparse aggregate interference to lie below a constant margin.

The distributional threshold result in Section 8 is likewise a random-dictionary support recovery statement. Its role is not to improve compressed-sensing theory, but to provide a clean comparison between two interface criteria: average linear readout error remains unavoidable under rank constraints, while threshold success depends on concentration of sparse aggregate interference.

3 Formal Model Definitions

We write O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot), Ω~​(⋅)\widetilde{\Omega}(\cdot), Θ~​(⋅)\widetilde{\Theta}(\cdot) to hide factors polynomial in log⁡d\log d or log⁡n\log n. Unless explicitly varied, s=O⁡(1)s=O(1) denotes a fixed constant sparsity parameter; Section 8 separately studies random supports with sparsity growing as large as O⁡(d/log⁡d)O(d/\log d).

Definition 3.1 (Model H: approximate-linear recursive template).

A recursive Model-H computation alternates: (i) a targeted superpositional AND computation layer producing outgoing error εcomp(d)=O~(d−1/2)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}(d)=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) under the hypotheses of the published Hänni template; and (ii) an error-correction layer (Theorem 21 of [7]) that tolerates incoming error εin<K⁡(d)​d1/4/(F1/2​s1/4)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}<K(d)\,d^{1/4}/(F^{1/2}s^{1/4}) and outputs εout,μout=O~​(s/d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}},\mu_{\mathrm{out}}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{s/d}). The recursion invariant is approximate ε\varepsilon-linear decodability with residual interference at each interface. We use Model H here to refer to this published computation–correction proof template, not to all possible ε\varepsilon-linear recursive algorithms.

Definition 3.2 (Model AS: threshold-reset recursive superposition).

In the Adler–Shavit framework [1], exact Boolean state is recovered by thresholding after each stage. The construction uses randomized compression/decompression so that the relevant scores separate active from inactive Boolean coordinates with a depth-independent margin. Their lower bound is a parameter-description lower bound, converted to a neuron lower bound under the architectural assumptions of their model, while their construction uses O⁡(m′​log⁡m′)O(\sqrt{m^{\prime}}\log m^{\prime}) neurons for m′m^{\prime} outputs. The recursion invariant is thresholded Boolean recovery, not small-error linear readout. We write FrecAS​(n)F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(n) for the corresponding recursive capacity.

Remark 3.3 (The essential distinction).

The key distinction is the recursion invariant: Model H maintains approximate ε\varepsilon-linear decodability with residual interference; Model AS restores exact Boolean state via thresholding, exiting the ε\varepsilon-linear class entirely.

4 Model H: The d3/2d^{3/2} Template Compatibility Threshold

Lemma 4.1 (Computation-layer interface for the Hänni template; [Imported]).

Fix s=O⁡(1)s=O(1) and suppose the targeted superpositional AND primitive of Hänni et al. (Theorem 11 of [7]) is applied in a regime satisfying its stated graph-balancing, sparsity, norm, and incoming-interference hypotheses. Then the computation layer used in that recursive template produces outgoing readout error

εcomp(d)=O~(s/d)=O~(d−1/2).\varepsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}(d)=\widetilde{O}(s/\sqrt{d})=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}).

This lemma is a restatement of the targeted computation primitive used by the template; it is not derived by substituting ε,μ=O~(d−1/2)\varepsilon,\mu=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) into the random-Gaussian Theorem 14 bound.

Proof.

Theorem 11 of Hänni et al., the targeted superpositional AND theorem, gives outgoing precision

εout=O~​(s2d)=O~​(s/d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{s^{2}}{d}}\right)=\widetilde{O}(s/\sqrt{d})

under its stated hypotheses, including the graph-balance and incoming-interference assumptions. For constant sparsity s=O⁡(1)s=O(1) this is O~(d−1/2)\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}).

The distinction from Theorem 14 is important. Theorem 14 gives an error term of the form

ε(1)=O~​(max⁡{s​μ,s​ε,s/d}).\varepsilon^{(1)}=\widetilde{O}\!\left(\max\{s\mu,\sqrt{s\varepsilon},\sqrt{s/d}\}\right).

If one only assumes ε,μ=O~(d−1/2)\varepsilon,\mu=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) and s=O⁡(1)s=O(1), then

s​ε=O~(d−1/4),\sqrt{s\varepsilon}=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/4}),

not O~(d−1/2)\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}). Thus Theorem 14 alone does not preserve the O~(d−1/2)\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) invariant. The present lemma records only the targeted computation-layer guarantee needed for the specific Hänni recursive template. ∎

Lemma 4.2 (Correction-layer tolerance; [Imported]).

The correction layer of Theorem 21 of [7] admits incoming error

εin<K⁡(d)​d1/4F1/2​s1/4,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}<K(d)\;\frac{d^{1/4}}{F^{1/2}\,s^{1/4}}, (1)

where K⁡(d)=polylog⁡(d)K(d)=\mathrm{polylog}(d), and produces corrected output with εout=O⁡((log⁡d)​s/d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}}=O((\log d)\sqrt{s/d}) and μout=O~​(s/d)\mu_{\mathrm{out}}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{s/d}).

Proposition 4.3 (Hänni-template compatibility threshold; [Derived]).

Fix s=O⁡(1)s=O(1). Consider the specific recursive template consisting of:

  1. 1.

    a computation layer with outgoing error εcomp(d)=O~(d−1/2)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}(d)=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) as in Lemma 4.1; and

  2. 2.

    the correction layer of Theorem 21 of Hänni et al., whose certified admissible incoming error is

    εcorr,max​(F,d,s)=K⁡(d)​d1/4F1/2​s1/4,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr,max}}(F,d,s)=K(d)\frac{d^{1/4}}{F^{1/2}s^{1/4}},

    and whose output satisfies εout,μout=O~​(s/d)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{out}},\mu_{\mathrm{out}}=\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{s/d}).

Then the published Hänni construction certifies recursive operation at feature load

F=Ω~​(d3/2).F=\widetilde{\Omega}(d^{3/2}).

Moreover, if one combines the computation-layer error certificate εcomp(d)=O~(d−1/2)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}(d)=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) with the stated correction-layer tolerance, the proof certificate applies in the regime

F≲O~​(d3/2).F\lesssim\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2}).

Thus d3/2d^{3/2} is the compatibility scale certified by this particular proof template. This proposition is not a universal upper bound for all ε\varepsilon-linear recursive interfaces.

Proof.

For this proof template, the published correction theorem is certified after the computation layer when

εcomp​(d)≲εcorr,max​(F,d,s).\varepsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}(d)\lesssim\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr,max}}(F,d,s).

Using Lemma 4.1 and s=O⁡(1)s=O(1), this condition becomes

O~(d−1/2)≲K(d)d1/4F1/2.\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2})\lesssim K(d)\frac{d^{1/4}}{F^{1/2}}.

Suppressing polylogarithmic factors,

F1/2≲d3/4,henceF≲O~​(d3/2).F^{1/2}\lesssim d^{3/4},\qquad\text{hence}\qquad F\lesssim\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2}).

Conversely, the recursive construction of Hänni et al. emulates constant-sparsity Boolean circuits of width mm using network width

d=O~​(m2/3​s2).d=\widetilde{O}(m^{2/3}s^{2}).

For s=O⁡(1)s=O(1), this gives a certified construction at m=Ω~​(d3/2)m=\widetilde{\Omega}(d^{3/2}). Therefore the published proof pipeline has a matching certified scale Θ~​(d3/2)\widetilde{\Theta}(d^{3/2}) as a template-specific certificate, rather than an impossibility result for other possible implementations. ∎

5 Model AS: Near-Quadratic Recursive Capacity

Proposition 5.1 (Model AS capacity upper bound; [Imported]).

In the Adler–Shavit framework, FrecAS​(n)≤O⁡(n2/log⁡n)F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(n)\leq O(n^{2}/\log n).

Proof.

The Adler–Shavit 2-AND parameter-description lower bound (Corollary 4.2.2 in their main text) states that any ε\varepsilon-correct computation of m′m^{\prime} 2-AND outputs requires parameter description length Ω⁡(m′​log⁡m′)\Omega(m^{\prime}\log m^{\prime}). For the square-matrix network model considered by Adler–Shavit, with Θ⁡(n2)\Theta(n^{2}) parameters and O⁡(1)O(1) average description length per parameter, this implies m′≤O⁡(n2/log⁡n)m^{\prime}\leq O(n^{2}/\log n). ∎

Proposition 5.2 (Model AS capacity lower bound; [Imported]).

There exists a construction using n=O⁡(F​log⁡F)n=O(\sqrt{F}\log F) neurons per stage with exact Boolean output. Therefore: FrecAS​(n)≥Ω⁡(n2/log2⁡n)F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(n)\geq\Omega(n^{2}/\log^{2}n).

Proof.

The constructive upper bound of [1] uses n=O⁡(m′​log⁡m′)n=O(\sqrt{m^{\prime}}\log m^{\prime}) neurons (note: log⁡m′\log m^{\prime}, not log⁡m′\sqrt{\log m^{\prime}}). Inverting: F=Ω⁡(n2/log2⁡n)F=\Omega(n^{2}/\log^{2}n). ∎

Corollary 5.3 (Model AS capacity bracket; [Derived]).

For recursive 2-AND computation at constant sparsity:

Ω⁡(n2/log2⁡n)≤FrecAS​(n)≤O⁡(n2/log⁡n).\Omega(n^{2}/\log^{2}n)\;\leq\;F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(n)\;\leq\;O(n^{2}/\log n). (2)

In particular, the capacity exponent is αA​S=2\alpha_{AS}=2 up to logarithmic factors. The gap of a single log\log factor between the upper and lower bounds is open; Adler and Shavit describe their construction as “within a log⁡m′\sqrt{\log m^{\prime}} factor of optimal.”

6 Model Comparison

Proposition 6.1 (Interface comparison; [Derived]).

Fix s=O⁡(1)s=O(1).

  1. (a)

    The Hänni approximate-linear recursive template has a certified compatibility scale

    FcertH​-​templ​(d)=Θ~​(d3/2)F_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}}(d)=\widetilde{\Theta}(d^{3/2})

    in the sense of Proposition 4.3.

  2. (b)

    In the Adler–Shavit setting, the parameter-description lower bound and the explicit construction imply the bracket

    Ω⁡(n2/log2⁡n)≤FrecAS​(n)≤O⁡(n2/log⁡n),\Omega(n^{2}/\log^{2}n)\leq F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(n)\leq O(n^{2}/\log n),

    under the architectural and parameter-description assumptions used to convert parameter complexity into neuron complexity.

  3. (c)

    The two regimes do not contradict each other. The Hänni template maintains an approximate ε\varepsilon-linear interface and must feed its residual error into a correction theorem whose certified tolerance is

    O~​(d1/4/F1/2).\widetilde{O}(d^{1/4}/F^{1/2}).

    Matching this tolerance to the unavoidable d−1/2d^{-1/2} linear cross-talk scale gives the d3/2d^{3/2} threshold for that template.

  4. (d)

    Adler–Shavit instead use thresholding to recover Boolean state with margin. This exits the small-error ε\varepsilon-linear readout invariant, so the Welch floor for linear cross-talk does not obstruct their exact-reset construction.

  5. (e)

    Ignoring logarithmic factors, the two templates have exponents 3/23/2 and 22, respectively. This exponent comparison is a comparison of known frameworks, not a theorem classifying all possible neural computations in superposition.

Proof.

Part (a) is Proposition 4.3. Part (b) follows from Adler–Shavit’s parameter-description lower bound Ω⁡(m′​log⁡m′)\Omega(m^{\prime}\log m^{\prime}) for the relevant 2-AND family, together with their explicit construction using n=O⁡(m′​log⁡m′)n=O(\sqrt{m^{\prime}}\log m^{\prime}) neurons. Inverting these bounds gives m′≤O⁡(n2/log⁡n)m^{\prime}\leq O(n^{2}/\log n) for the lower-bound side and m′≥Ω⁡(n2/log2⁡n)m^{\prime}\geq\Omega(n^{2}/\log^{2}n) for the construction side. Parts (c) and (d) identify the different recursion invariants, and part (e) is only an asymptotic comparison of these two frameworks. ∎

7 The Biorthogonal Welch Floor

We now prove the main unconditional result of the paper: a rank–trace Welch-type lower bound for linear readouts. The theorem is purely geometric. It does not by itself prove a recursive capacity upper bound. Its role is to show that any interface that remains linearly readable in dimension dd with F≫dF\gg d features must incur worst-case cross-talk of order at least d−1/2d^{-1/2}.

Theorem 7.1 (Biorthogonal Welch Floor; [Proved]).

Let F≥2F\geq 2 and let Ψ=[ψ1,…,ψF]∈ℝd×F\Psi=[\psi_{1},\ldots,\psi_{F}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times F} be any code matrix. Let G∈ℝF×dG\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times d} be any linear readout matrix and set M:=G​ΨM:=G\Psi. Suppose

Mi​i=(G​Ψ)i​i=1for all ​i∈[F].M_{ii}=(G\Psi)_{ii}=1\qquad\text{for all }i\in[F].

Then

∑i≠j|(G​Ψ)i​j|2≥F⁡(F−d)d.\sum_{i\neq j}|(G\Psi)_{ij}|^{2}\geq\frac{F(F-d)}{d}. (3)

Consequently, if F>dF>d, then

1F⁡(F−1)​∑i≠j|(G​Ψ)i​j|2≥F−dd⁡(F−1),\frac{1}{F(F-1)}\sum_{i\neq j}|(G\Psi)_{ij}|^{2}\geq\frac{F-d}{d(F-1)}, (4)

and hence

maxi≠j⁡|(G​Ψ)i​j|≥F−dd⁡(F−1).\max_{i\neq j}|(G\Psi)_{ij}|\geq\sqrt{\frac{F-d}{d(F-1)}}. (5)

In particular, if F/d→∞F/d\to\infty, then

maxi≠j|(GΨ)i​j|≥(1−o(1))d−1/2.\max_{i\neq j}|(G\Psi)_{ij}|\geq(1-o(1))d^{-1/2}.

If F=κ​d2F=\kappa d^{2} for fixed κ>0\kappa>0, then

maxi≠j|(GΨ)i​j|=Ω(d−1/2).\max_{i\neq j}|(G\Psi)_{ij}|=\Omega(d^{-1/2}).
Proof.

Since M=G​ΨM=G\Psi with G∈ℝF×dG\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times d} and Ψ∈ℝd×F\Psi\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times F},

rank⁡(M)≤d.\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq d.

Also, by the unit-diagonal assumption,

tr⁡(M)=F.\operatorname{tr}(M)=F.

‖M‖F2=∑i|Mi​i|2+∑i≠j|Mi​j|2=F+∑i≠j|Mi​j|2.\|M\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{i}|M_{ii}|^{2}+\sum_{i\neq j}|M_{ij}|^{2}=F+\sum_{i\neq j}|M_{ij}|^{2}.

This proves (3). If F>dF>d, division by F⁡(F−1)F(F-1) gives (4), and the maximum lower bound follows because the maximum of nonnegative numbers is at least their average square root. ∎

Proposition 7.2 (Average tightness for unit-norm tight frames; [Proved]).

Corollary 7.4 (No better-than-Welch ε\varepsilon-linear reset).

Let F>dF>d and let y1,…,yF∈ℝdy_{1},\ldots,y_{F}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be singleton output states. Suppose there is a common linear readout G∈ℝF×dG\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times d} such that

and M~=D​G​Y\widetilde{M}=DGY. Since δd<1/2\delta_{d}<1/2, all diagonal entries are nonzero, and M~i​i=1\widetilde{M}_{ii}=1. Moreover, for i≠ji\neq j,

For F/d→∞F/d\to\infty, the right-hand side is (1−o(1))d−1/2(1-o(1))d^{-1/2}. ∎

Remark 7.5.

Corollary 7.4 rules out resets that remain in the small-error ε\varepsilon-linear readout class. It does not rule out nonlinear threshold decoders, discrete state recovery, or distribution-specific average-case mechanisms.

7.1 Why threshold reset does not contradict the Welch floor

The Welch floor lower-bounds worst-case off-diagonal cross-talk for linear readout matrices with unit diagonal. It therefore rules out small-error ε\varepsilon-linear reset with ε=o(d−1/2)\varepsilon=o(d^{-1/2}) when F≫dF\gg d. It does not, however, rule out thresholded Boolean recovery.

The reason is simple: threshold recovery does not require every inactive score to be o(d−1/2)o(d^{-1/2}). It only requires the aggregate interference from the active sparse support to remain below the threshold margin. The following standard coherence/support-recovery lemma makes this distinction explicit. It is included as an illustrative invariant-separation result; it is not a construction of the Adler–Shavit reset layer.

Theorem 7.6 (Threshold recovery under coherent superposition; [Proved]).

Let

Φ=[ϕ1,…,ϕF]∈ℝd×F\Phi=[\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{F}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times F}

μ:=maxi≠j⁡|⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩|.\mu:=\max_{i\neq j}|\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle|.

‖Φ⊤​η‖∞≤ν.\|\Phi^{\top}\eta\|_{\infty}\leq\nu.

Q(z)i:=𝟏{zi≥1/2}.Q(z)_{i}:=\mathbf{1}\{z_{i}\geq 1/2\}.

then

τ:=12−(s​μ+ν)>0,\tau:=\frac{1}{2}-(s\mu+\nu)>0,

bi=1⇒zi≥12+τ,bi=0⇒zi≤12−τ.b_{i}=1\Rightarrow z_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}+\tau,\qquad b_{i}=0\Rightarrow z_{i}\leq\frac{1}{2}-\tau.

Let

the score of coordinate ii is

zi=⟨ϕi,x⟩=∑j∈S⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩+⟨ϕi,η⟩.z_{i}=\langle\phi_{i},x\rangle=\sum_{j\in S}\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle+\langle\phi_{i},\eta\rangle.

First suppose i∈Si\in S. Then

zi=1+∑j∈Sj≠i⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩+⟨ϕi,η⟩.z_{i}=1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in S\\ j\neq i\end{subarray}}\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle+\langle\phi_{i},\eta\rangle.

Therefore Q⁡(z)=bQ(z)=b, and the displayed margin bounds hold for every coordinate. ∎

it is enough that

‖Φ⊤​η‖∞<12−C0​s​log⁡dd.\|\Phi^{\top}\eta\|_{\infty}<\frac{1}{2}-C_{0}s\sqrt{\frac{\log d}{d}}.

For fixed s=O⁡(1)s=O(1), the term s​log⁡d/ds\sqrt{\log d/d} tends to zero, so in the noiseless case the threshold condition holds for all sufficiently large dd. The final statement follows because Corollary 7.4 rules out only small-error ε\varepsilon-linear recovery, not thresholded Boolean recovery. ∎

Remark 7.8.

Theorem 7.6 is a coherence-based support-recovery lemma. It does not construct a recursive reset module, does not prove Hypothesis 9.1, and does not reproduce the Adler–Shavit construction. Its purpose is narrower: it shows, in a self-contained way, why thresholded Boolean recovery can coexist with unavoidable linear cross-talk.

Remark 7.9 (Connection to spectral localization).

Ivanov et al. [8] study spectral localization and tight-frame-like structure in capacity-saturated toy models of superposition. This is related geometric context for the Welch floor: tight frames are configurations that can asymptotically saturate Welch-type bounds. Our theorem, however, does not assume spectral localization and does not imply that trained models generically operate in this extremal regime.

8 Distributional Separation Between Linear Readout and Threshold Recovery

The previous section compared worst-case linear cross-talk with worst-case coherence-based threshold recovery. We now give a distributional comparison. The first result shows that the Welch floor also implies a nontrivial average linear readout error for random sparse Boolean states. The second result shows that, for random dictionaries and random supports, threshold recovery succeeds at much larger sparsities than the worst-case coherence bound certifies.

These results are closely related to standard random-dictionary and compressed-sensing support-recovery arguments. We include them not as new compressed-sensing theorems, but to sharpen the interface distinction: small linear readout error and thresholded Boolean recovery are different criteria.

Lemma 8.2 (Subgaussian interference for random unit vectors).

There exist universal constants c0,C0>0c_{0},C_{0}>0 such that the following holds. Let u,u1,…,umu,u_{1},\ldots,u_{m} be independent random unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. If m=0m=0, then

∑j=1m⟨u,uj⟩=0.\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle u,u_{j}\rangle=0.

Pr{|∑j=1m⟨u,uj⟩|>t}≤2exp(−c0d​t2m).\Pr\!\left\{\left|\sum_{j=1}^{m}\langle u,u_{j}\rangle\right|>t\right\}\leq 2\exp\!\left(-c_{0}\frac{dt^{2}}{m}\right).

Xj:=⟨u,uj⟩X_{j}:=\langle u,u_{j}\rangle

𝔼⁡[Xj∣u]=0,\mathbb{E}[X_{j}\mid u]=0,

and the random variables X1,…,XmX_{1},\ldots,X_{m} are conditionally independent.

The standard spherical-cap estimate gives universal constants c,C>0c,C>0 such that, for all a>0a>0,

Pr⁡{|Xj|>a∣u}≤C​exp⁡(−c​d​a2).\Pr\{|X_{j}|>a\mid u\}\leq C\exp(-cda^{2}).

For each i∈[F]i\in[F], define

Ii​(S,Φ):=∑j∈Sj≠i⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩.I_{i}(S,\Phi):=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in S\\ j\neq i\end{subarray}}\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle.

Condition on the support SS. For a fixed ii, the sum defining IiI_{i} contains at most ss terms. Moreover, the vectors appearing in the sum are independent of ϕi\phi_{i}, since the term j=ij=i is omitted. Thus Lemma 8.2 implies that for every t>0t>0,

Pr⁡{|Ii​(S,Φ)|>t∣S}≤2​exp⁡(−c0​d​t2s),\Pr\{|I_{i}(S,\Phi)|>t\mid S\}\leq 2\exp\!\left(-c_{0}\frac{dt^{2}}{s}\right),

where c0>0c_{0}>0 is a universal constant. This bound also holds when i∈Si\in S, because then the sum has at most s−1s-1 terms; using ss only weakens the estimate.

Taking a union bound over i∈[F]i\in[F] gives

Pr⁡{maxi∈[F]⁡|Ii​(S,Φ)|>t|S}≤2​F​exp⁡(−c0​d​t2s).\Pr\!\left\{\max_{i\in[F]}|I_{i}(S,\Phi)|>t\middle|S\right\}\leq 2F\exp\!\left(-c_{0}\frac{dt^{2}}{s}\right).

Choose

t=C​s​log⁡(F/δ)dt=C\sqrt{\frac{s\log(F/\delta)}{d}}

with C>0C>0 large enough that

2​F​exp⁡(−c0​C2​log⁡(F/δ))≤δ2F\exp\!\left(-c_{0}C^{2}\log(F/\delta)\right)\leq\delta

for all F≥2F\geq 2 and δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1). Hence

Pr⁡{maxi∈[F]⁡|Ii​(S,Φ)|≤C​s​log⁡(F/δ)d|S}≥1−δ.\Pr\!\left\{\max_{i\in[F]}|I_{i}(S,\Phi)|\leq C\sqrt{\frac{s\log(F/\delta)}{d}}\middle|S\right\}\geq 1-\delta.

Since this bound holds for every fixed support SS, it also holds when SS is uniformly random and independent of Φ\Phi.

Now suppose the displayed interference bound holds, and define

ν:=‖Φ⊤​η‖∞,t:=C​s​log⁡(F/δ)d.\nu:=\|\Phi^{\top}\eta\|_{\infty},\qquad t:=C\sqrt{\frac{s\log(F/\delta)}{d}}.

For i∈Si\in S,

zi=⟨ϕi,x⟩=1+∑j∈Sj≠i⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩+⟨ϕi,η⟩≥1−t−ν.z_{i}=\langle\phi_{i},x\rangle=1+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in S\\ j\neq i\end{subarray}}\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle+\langle\phi_{i},\eta\rangle\geq 1-t-\nu.

For i∉Si\notin S,

zi=∑j∈S⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩+⟨ϕi,η⟩≤t+ν.z_{i}=\sum_{j\in S}\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle+\langle\phi_{i},\eta\rangle\leq t+\nu.

If

then every active coordinate has score strictly larger than 1/21/2, and every inactive coordinate has score strictly smaller than 1/21/2. Thus thresholding at level 1/21/2 exactly recovers 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S}. ∎

Corollary 8.4 (Quadratic-load distributional separation; [Proved]).

This corollary compares two distinct sparse-state models: a uniformly random support of fixed size ss for the threshold-recovery side, and independent Bernoulli coordinates of expected sparsity ss for the linear-readout side. It is therefore not a pointwise comparison on a single draw of bb, but a comparison of two interface criteria under their natural sparse-state distributions.

Let

F=d2F=d^{2}

and let ϕ1,…,ϕF\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{F} be independent random unit vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Let S⊆[F]S\subseteq[F] be a uniformly random support of size ss, independent of the code. There exists a universal constant c>0c>0 such that, if

1≤s≤c​dlog⁡d,1\leq s\leq c\frac{d}{\log d},

then, in the noiseless case

x=Φ​𝟏S,x=\Phi\mathbf{1}_{S},

thresholding Φ⊤​x\Phi^{\top}x at level 1/21/2 recovers 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S} with probability at least

1−d−101-d^{-10}

for all sufficiently large dd.

At the same quadratic feature load, every linear readout interface M=G​ΨM=G\Psi with

rank⁡(M)≤d,Mi​i=1,\operatorname{rank}(M)\leq d,\qquad M_{ii}=1,

has the following average-error lower bound under Bernoulli sparse states: if bi∼Bernoulli⁡(s/F)b_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(s/F) independently and A=M−IFA=M-I_{F}, then

1F​𝔼b​‖A​b‖22≥Ω⁡(sd).\frac{1}{F}\mathbb{E}_{b}\|Ab\|_{2}^{2}\geq\Omega\!\left(\frac{s}{d}\right).

Thus, at F=d2F=d^{2}, random-support threshold recovery can succeed for s=O⁡(d/log⁡d)s=O(d/\log d) even though linear readout interfaces retain average per-coordinate squared error of order at least s/ds/d under Bernoulli sparse states. This compares two different interface criteria: linear readout error and threshold success.

Proof.

Apply Theorem 8.3 with

F=d2,δ=d−10.F=d^{2},\qquad\delta=d^{-10}.

log⁡(F/δ)=log⁡(d12)=12​log⁡d.\log(F/\delta)=\log(d^{12})=12\log d.

maxi∈[F]⁡|∑j∈Sj≠i⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩|≤C​12​s​log⁡dd\max_{i\in[F]}\left|\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\in S\\ j\neq i\end{subarray}}\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle\right|\leq C\sqrt{\frac{12s\log d}{d}}

with probability at least 1−d−101-d^{-10}.

Choose a universal constant c>0c>0 small enough that

C​12​c<12.C\sqrt{12c}<\frac{1}{2}.

For example, any

c<148​C2c<\frac{1}{48C^{2}}

suffices. If

s≤c​dlog⁡d,s\leq c\frac{d}{\log d},

then

C​12​s​log⁡dd≤C​12​c<12.C\sqrt{\frac{12s\log d}{d}}\leq C\sqrt{12c}<\frac{1}{2}.

In the noiseless case η=0\eta=0, the threshold condition of Theorem 8.3 is therefore satisfied, and thresholding Φ⊤​x\Phi^{\top}x at 1/21/2 recovers 𝟏S\mathbf{1}_{S}.

For the linear-readout lower bound, apply Theorem 8.1 with F=d2F=d^{2} and p=s/Fp=s/F. Since s≤c​d/log⁡d≤F/2s\leq cd/\log d\leq F/2 for all sufficiently large dd, the specialization in Theorem 8.1 gives

1F​𝔼b​‖A​b‖22≥s⁡(F−d)2​d​F.\frac{1}{F}\mathbb{E}_{b}\|Ab\|_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{s(F-d)}{2dF}.

Substituting F=d2F=d^{2},

s⁡(F−d)2​d​F=s⁡(d2−d)2​d3=s2​d​(1−1d)=Ω⁡(sd).\frac{s(F-d)}{2dF}=\frac{s(d^{2}-d)}{2d^{3}}=\frac{s}{2d}\left(1-\frac{1}{d}\right)=\Omega\!\left(\frac{s}{d}\right).

This proves the claimed distributional comparison.

The two sparse-state models used here are intentionally distinguished: the threshold-recovery statement uses a uniformly random support of fixed size ss, while the linear-energy lower bound uses independent Bernoulli coordinates with expected sparsity ss. Both are standard sparse input models, but the corollary should not be read as a pointwise comparison on the same draw of bb. ∎

What this distributional separation does and does not prove.

Corollary 8.4 is a separation between two interface criteria. It shows that, at quadratic feature load, linear readout can retain nontrivial average energy error on random sparse states while threshold recovery succeeds for random supports of size O⁡(d/log⁡d)O(d/\log d) in a random dictionary. It does not give uniform recovery over all supports, does not construct a recursive reset module, does not prove Hypothesis 9.1, and does not imply a universal lower bound on computation in superposition. In particular, it does not claim a universal d3/2d^{3/2} impossibility theorem. Its role is to make explicit that small-error linear readout and thresholded Boolean recovery are genuinely different invariants.

9 Open-Problem Framework: Nonlinear Reset Interpolation

This section is an open-problem framework, not a substantive theorem. Sections 7 and 8 establish the interface distinction used below. First, a reset which remains in the small-error ε\varepsilon-linear readout class cannot improve the worst-case linear cross-talk scale beyond d−1/2d^{-1/2} when F≫dF\gg d. Second, thresholded Boolean recovery can succeed under sparse aggregate interference without requiring small-error ℓ∞\ell_{\infty} linear recovery; in the random-support setting, this remains true at quadratic feature load for sparsities up to O⁡(d/log⁡d)O(d/\log d). Therefore any interpolation beyond the Hänni approximate-linear template must leave the small-error ε\varepsilon-linear class.

Below, γ>0\gamma>0 denotes a hypothetical gain in nonlinear or thresholded reset tolerance, not an improvement to ε\varepsilon-linear output error. The statement we record (Proposition 9.3) is essentially an algebraic rewriting of Hypothesis 9.1: it says that if a reset interface with input-error tolerance scaling as d1/4+γ/2d^{1/4+\gamma/2} existed, then matching it to the computation-layer error d−1/2d^{-1/2} would give feature load O~​(d3/2+γ)\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2+\gamma}). The mathematical content lies entirely in the hypothesis, which for γ>0\gamma>0 is conjectural and not known to be instantiable. We include this calculation only to make quantitative the open question that follows.

Hypothesis 9.1 (Nonlinear γ\gamma-reset interface; [Conjectured]).

Fix γ∈[0,1/2]\gamma\in[0,1/2] and s=O⁡(1)s=O(1). A nonlinear γ\gamma-reset interface consists of a reset map

𝒞γ:ℝd→ℝd,\mathcal{C}_{\gamma}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d},

a linear scoring map

Rγ∈ℝF×d,R_{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times d},

and a threshold decoder

Qγ(z)i:=𝟏{(Rγz)i≥1/2},i∈[F],Q_{\gamma}(z)_{i}:=\mathbf{1}\{(R_{\gamma}z)_{i}\geq 1/2\},\qquad i\in[F],

with the following properties.

  1. (i)

    Admissible input error. If an input state represents an ss-sparse Boolean vector b∈{0,1}Fb\in\{0,1\}^{F} with incoming interface error εin\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}, and

    εin≤Kγ​(d)​d1/4+γ/2F1/2​s1/4,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}\leq K_{\gamma}(d)\,\frac{d^{1/4+\gamma/2}}{F^{1/2}s^{1/4}},

    then the reset may be applied.

  2. (ii)

    Threshold recovery with margin. There exists a margin τγ​(d)>0\tau_{\gamma}(d)>0 such that, for z=𝒞γ​(x)z=\mathcal{C}_{\gamma}(x),

    bi=1⟹(Rγ​z)i≥12+τγ​(d),b_{i}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(R_{\gamma}z)_{i}\geq\frac{1}{2}+\tau_{\gamma}(d),

    and

    bi=0⟹(Rγ​z)i≤12−τγ​(d).b_{i}=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad(R_{\gamma}z)_{i}\leq\frac{1}{2}-\tau_{\gamma}(d).

    Equivalently,

    Qγ​(𝒞γ​(x))=b.Q_{\gamma}(\mathcal{C}_{\gamma}(x))=b.
  3. (iii)

    Composability. The reset output belongs to the input class accepted by the next computation layer in the template, and that computation layer again produces outgoing error O~(d−1/2)\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) on the next Boolean state.

For γ=0\gamma=0, this hypothesis may be instantiated by the approximate-linear Hänni correction layer. For γ>0\gamma>0, it is explicitly a nonlinear or threshold-reset hypothesis. It does not claim that

∥Rγ𝒞γ(x)−b∥∞=O(d−1/2−γ),\|R_{\gamma}\mathcal{C}_{\gamma}(x)-b\|_{\infty}=O(d^{-1/2-\gamma}),

which would contradict Theorem 7.1 when F≫dF\gg d.

Remark 9.2.

The exponent d1/4+γ/2d^{1/4+\gamma/2} is a parametrization of input tolerance. It is chosen so that matching the computation-layer error d−1/2d^{-1/2} to the reset tolerance gives the formal exponent 3/2+γ3/2+\gamma. It is not derived from existing constructions for γ>0\gamma>0.

Proposition 9.3 (Conditional nonlinear-reset interpolation calculation; [Conditional]).

Fix s=O⁡(1)s=O(1) and assume Hypothesis 9.1 holds for some γ∈[0,1/2]\gamma\in[0,1/2]. Then the corresponding computation–reset template is certified for feature loads

F≤O~​(d3/2+γ).F\leq\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2+\gamma}).

More precisely, for any

F≤cγ​Kγ​(d)2​d3/2+γs1/2,F\leq c_{\gamma}\,\frac{K_{\gamma}(d)^{2}\,d^{3/2+\gamma}}{s^{1/2}},

with cγ>0c_{\gamma}>0 sufficiently small, the computation-layer error O~(d−1/2)\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}) lies within the admissible input tolerance of the reset, and the threshold decoder recovers the Boolean state after each reset step.

This is an algebraic calculation conditional on Hypothesis 9.1. For γ>0\gamma>0, it is not a theorem about ε\varepsilon-linear reset layers and not a universal upper bound. Its mathematical content is encapsulated in the hypothesis, which remains open.

Proof.

By the composability assumption, each computation layer produces outgoing error

εin=O~(d−1/2).\varepsilon_{\mathrm{in}}=\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2}).

The reset can be applied when

O~(d−1/2)≤Kγ(d)d1/4+γ/2F1/2​s1/4.\widetilde{O}(d^{-1/2})\leq K_{\gamma}(d)\frac{d^{1/4+\gamma/2}}{F^{1/2}s^{1/4}}.

Rearranging gives

F1/2≤O~​(Kγ​(d)​d3/4+γ/2s1/4),F^{1/2}\leq\widetilde{O}\!\left(K_{\gamma}(d)\frac{d^{3/4+\gamma/2}}{s^{1/4}}\right),

and hence

F≤O~​(Kγ​(d)2​d3/2+γs1/2).F\leq\widetilde{O}\!\left(\frac{K_{\gamma}(d)^{2}\,d^{3/2+\gamma}}{s^{1/2}}\right).

Under this condition, Hypothesis 9.1 gives exact threshold recovery of the Boolean state with margin τγ​(d)\tau_{\gamma}(d) after each reset. The composability clause then allows the next computation layer to be applied, so the cycle can be iterated.

No converse is proved: failure of this inequality only means that this hypothesized interface no longer certifies the recursion. ∎

10 Capacity Taxonomy

Different notions of “capacity” in superposition measure different objects. The following reference-scale comparison is intended as a taxonomy only: the quantities count different objects and should not be read as a single universal capacity ordering.

Remark 10.1 (Reference-scale comparison).

Fix s=O⁡(1)s=O(1), fixed sparsity α∈(0,1)\alpha\in(0,1), and fixed ε>0\varepsilon>0. Define

FCS​(d,α):=d​g​(α),g⁡(α):=1(1−α)​ln⁡(1/(1−α)).F_{\mathrm{CS}}(d,\alpha):=d\,g(\alpha),\qquad g(\alpha):=\frac{1}{(1-\alpha)\ln(1/(1-\alpha))}.

Fix constants A,cH,CH>0A,c_{H},C_{H}>0 and let FcertH​-​templ​(d)F_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}}(d) be any positive reference function satisfying

cH​d3/2(log⁡d)A≤FcertH​-​templ​(d)≤CH​d3/2​(log⁡d)A.c_{H}\,\frac{d^{3/2}}{(\log d)^{A}}\leq F_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}}(d)\leq C_{H}\,d^{3/2}(\log d)^{A}.

Define the lower and upper sides of the Adler–Shavit bracket by

LAS​(d):=d2(log⁡d)2,UAS​(d):=d2log⁡d.L_{\mathrm{AS}}(d):=\frac{d^{2}}{(\log d)^{2}},\qquad U_{\mathrm{AS}}(d):=\frac{d^{2}}{\log d}.

Assume the Adler–Shavit capacity satisfies

FrecAS​(d)≥c​LAS​(d),FrecAS​(d)≤C​UAS​(d)F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(d)\geq c\,L_{\mathrm{AS}}(d),\qquad F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}(d)\leq C\,U_{\mathrm{AS}}(d)

for constants c,C>0c,C>0 in the relevant asymptotic regime. Finally let

NJL​(d,ε):=exp⁡(Θ⁡(d​ε2)).N_{\mathrm{JL}}(d;\varepsilon):=\exp(\Theta(d\varepsilon^{2})).

Then, as d→∞d\to\infty,

FCS​(d,α)=o⁡(FcertH​-​templ​(d)),F_{\mathrm{CS}}(d,\alpha)=o\!\left(F_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}}(d)\right),
FcertH​-​templ​(d)=o⁡(LAS​(d)),F_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}}(d)=o\!\left(L_{\mathrm{AS}}(d)\right),

and

UAS​(d)=o⁡(NJL​(d,ε)).U_{\mathrm{AS}}(d)=o\!\left(N_{\mathrm{JL}}(d;\varepsilon)\right).

Thus the reference scales obey the asymptotic order

FCS≪FcertH​-​templ≪LAS≲FrecAS≲UAS≪NJL,F_{\mathrm{CS}}\ll F_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}}\ll L_{\mathrm{AS}}\lesssim F_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}\lesssim U_{\mathrm{AS}}\ll N_{\mathrm{JL}},

where the middle inequalities use the lower and upper sides of the Adler–Shavit bracket, and FcertH​-​templF_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}} has the template-specific interpretation of Proposition 4.3.

The crossover widths between compressed-sensing-style storage and the reference recursive-computation scales are:

dCS×H\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{CS\times H}} =g​(α)2,\displaystyle=g(\alpha)^{2}, (6)
dCS×AS\displaystyle d_{\mathrm{CS\times AS}} :d/log2d=g(α)for the lower-side AS reference scale.\displaystyle:\quad d/\log^{2}d=g(\alpha)\quad\text{for the lower-side AS reference scale.} (7)
Remark 10.2 (Numerical crossover values).

For α=0.99\alpha=0.99: g⁡(0.99)≈21.7g(0.99)\approx 21.7 and dCS×H≈472d_{\mathrm{CS\times H}}\approx 472. For α=0.992\alpha=0.992: g⁡(0.992)≈25.9g(0.992)\approx 25.9 and dCS×H≈670d_{\mathrm{CS\times H}}\approx 670. The AS crossover in (7) is only a lower-bracket reference scale and depends logarithmically on the convention for log\log and on the unresolved AS log gap; we therefore do not attach interpretive weight to its small-dd numerical value.

Remark 10.3 (Interpretation).

The hierarchy does not mean “recursive computation beats storage.” These bounds count different objects: NJLN_{\mathrm{JL}} counts passively packable states; FCSF_{\mathrm{CS}} counts linearly decodable features through a compressed bottleneck; FcertH​-​templF_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}} and FrecASF_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}} count recursively computable Boolean features under two different published frameworks. Beyond the crossover width, the bottleneck for internal recursive computation is looser than for one-shot linearly decodable storage, reflecting a difference in task definition, not a contradiction. Michaud et al. [12] provide a complementary explanation for why FobsF_{\mathrm{obs}} may fall below the d3/2d^{3/2} template scale: if feature manifolds consume capacity, the relevant comparison is Deff:=∑iqiD_{\mathrm{eff}}:=\sum_{i}q_{i} against that template scale, not simply FF.

11 Open Problem: Robust Threshold Reset

The interpolation identifies a concrete open problem: whether a correction layer with γ>0\gamma>0 can be explicitly constructed.

Conjecture 11.1 (Generic robust threshold reset; [Conjectured]).

Fix s=O⁡(1)s=O(1). There exist constants c,C,K>0c,C,K>0 such that for every dd and every

F≤c​d2/logC⁡d,F\leq c\,d^{2}/\log^{C}d,

there are an input code Φ∈ℝd×F\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times F}, an input readout Rin∈ℝF×dR_{\mathrm{in}}\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times d}, a width-O~​(d)\widetilde{O}(d) reset module

ℛΦ:ℝd→ℝd,\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d},

an output code Φ′∈ℝd×F\Phi^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times F}, and a scoring map S∈ℝF×dS\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times d} with the following property.

For every ss-sparse 𝐛∈{0,1}F\mathbf{b}\in\{0,1\}^{F} and every input state x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} satisfying the incoming interface-error condition

‖Rin​x−𝐛‖∞≤K​d1/2F1/2​s1/4,\|R_{\mathrm{in}}x-\mathbf{b}\|_{\infty}\leq K\,\frac{d^{1/2}}{F^{1/2}s^{1/4}},

the reset output z=ℛΦ​(x)z=\mathcal{R}_{\Phi}(x) is composable with the next stage, and its scores recover 𝐛\mathbf{b} with constant margin:

bi=1⇒(S​z)i≥1/2+1/4,bi=0⇒(S​z)i≤1/2−1/4.b_{i}=1\Rightarrow(Sz)_{i}\geq 1/2+1/4,\qquad b_{i}=0\Rightarrow(Sz)_{i}\leq 1/2-1/4.

No condition of the form ∥Sz−𝐛∥∞=o(d−1/2)\|Sz-\mathbf{b}\|_{\infty}=o(d^{-1/2}) is assumed.

A conjecture of this form would instantiate the γ=1/2\gamma=1/2 endpoint of the conditional interpolation framework because it includes the required incoming-error tolerance. A reset theorem for clean inputs x=Φ​𝐛x=\Phi\mathbf{b} alone would not be sufficient for recursive composition. Corollary 7.4 shows that achieving this endpoint within the small-error ε\varepsilon-linear class is impossible; therefore, any proof must employ an explicitly non-linear or thresholded decoding mechanism, as Adler–Shavit do via thresholding.

12 Empirical Context

The formal results above are worst-case statements about sparse Boolean interfaces. Appendix A collects SAE-related observations and scaling heuristics as motivational context only. These observations concern linearly reconstructive dictionaries and do not measure recursive Boolean computation capacity.

13 Discussion

Relation to open problems.

[15] identify as open the question of “what new theoretical insights can be gleaned from considering how networks perform computation natively in superposition.” Our work addresses one mathematical aspect of this question through a linear-interface cross-talk floor and a conditional reset framework.

What the linear-interface floor does and does not show.

Theorem 7.1 does not use tight frames, ReLU nonlinearities, or a particular correction architecture. It applies to any interface whose outputs remain linearly readable in dimension dd with unit diagonal. However, it is a geometric floor on linear readout cross-talk, not a universal lower bound on all recursive computation in superposition. Nonlinear threshold decoders and distribution-specific average-case mechanisms may evade the obstruction.

Empirical context.

The companion-study SAE measurements are used only as motivation for thinking about superposed dictionaries. They are not evidence for the formal exponents in this paper: SAE dictionary size measures a reconstructive latent dictionary, whereas our theorems concern linear readout floors, threshold recovery, and recursive Boolean interface criteria.

The storable/computable distinction.

The reference-scale comparison (Remark 10.1) summarizes that storing features (FCSF_{\mathrm{CS}}), computing with them recursively under a specific template (FcertH​-​templF_{\mathrm{cert}}^{\mathrm{H\text{-}templ}}, FrecASF_{\mathrm{rec}}^{\mathrm{AS}}), and merely representing them (NJLN_{\mathrm{JL}}) are distinct tasks with different capacity scales.

SAE scaling caveat.

Public SAE results provide useful context for superposition, but they should not be interpreted as measurements of recursive computation capacity. In particular, the theory here does not predict a universal SAE dictionary size, nor does it infer reset mechanisms from observed numbers of learned latents.

Limitations.

(i) The Hänni-template comparison assumes constant-sparsity Boolean computation, while the distributional threshold result separately treats random supports with ss growing up to O⁡(d/log⁡d)O(d/\log d); real features are continuous with heterogeneous sparsity. (ii) The Welch floor bounds small-error linear readout interfaces, not all possible corrections. (iii) The interpolation (Proposition 9.3) is conditional on Hypothesis 9.1 for γ>0\gamma>0. (iv) Empirical data uses fixed F=8​dF=8d, precluding direct estimation of α\alpha. (v) The AS capacity bracket has a log\log-factor gap that is open.

14 Conclusion

We have clarified a geometric obstruction that applies to linear interfaces for computation in superposition. The main theorem is a Biorthogonal Welch Floor: any dimension-dd code with F>dF>d features and a unit-diagonal linear readout must have average squared off-diagonal cross-talk at least (F−d)/(d⁡(F−1))(F-d)/(d(F-1)). Consequently, when F≫dF\gg d, worst-case linear cross-talk cannot be o(d−1/2)o(d^{-1/2}).

This floor explains why the published Hänni recursive proof certificate naturally stops at the d3/2d^{3/2} scale: its computation-layer error estimate must fit within a correction theorem with certified tolerance d1/4/F1/2d^{1/4}/F^{1/2}. Matching the two gives F≲O~​(d3/2)F\lesssim\widetilde{O}(d^{3/2}). This is a compatibility scale for that approximate-linear proof template, not a universal upper bound for all neural computation in superposition.

The Adler–Shavit construction avoids this obstruction by changing the recursion invariant. Instead of maintaining a small-error ε\varepsilon-linear interface, it uses thresholding to recover Boolean state with margin. The coherence-based and distributional threshold-recovery results above illustrate why this is mathematically possible: exact Boolean recovery requires sparse aggregate interference to remain below a constant threshold, not every off-diagonal linear score to be o(d−1/2)o(d^{-1/2}). In the random-support model, this distinction persists at quadratic feature load for support sizes up to O⁡(d/log⁡d)O(d/\log d), while linear readout interfaces still incur average energy error. This accounts for why thresholded recovery is not obstructed by the same linear-readout floor that constrains the Hänni approximate-linear template.

The conditional nonlinear reset framework in Section 9 should be read as an open-problem formulation. For γ>0\gamma>0, such a reset must leave the small-error ε\varepsilon-linear class; otherwise it would contradict the Welch floor. Proving or refuting the existence of such nonlinear resets is the central mathematical question left open by this work.

The empirical SAE discussion is therefore motivational rather than evidential. Current sparse autoencoder measurements may suggest where to look for reset-like or threshold-like mechanisms, but they do not establish the capacity exponents proved or conjectured here.

Appendix A SAE Motivation and Scaling Heuristics

A.1 SAE Data from Companion Study

As motivational context, we report data from [2]: TopK SAEs (k=64k=64, expansion 8​d8d) on Gemma 3 1B (d=1152d=1152), Gemma 2 2B (d=2304d=2304), and Llama 3.2 1B (d=2048d=2048). All models show zero dead features at F=8​dF=8d, placing these dictionaries below the d3/2d^{3/2} Hänni-template scale and the near-quadratic Adler–Shavit scale (Table 1). This is contextual only; SAE dictionary size is not a direct measurement of recursive computation capacity.

A.2 Qualitative Consistency with Theory

Rare SAE features (low firing rate) survive weight pruning better than frequent ones (ρ=−1.0\rho=-1.0 in 11/17 conditions [2]). This structured survival pattern may be consistent with features occupying non-uniform roles in an approximate code, but it is not diagnostic of the formal interface model: pruning survival also depends on frequency, magnitude, optimizer dynamics, and circuit importance.

A.3 Testable Predictions

Prediction A.1 (Capacity exponent ⇒\Rightarrow scaling-law slope; [Conjectured]).

Suppose feature importances follow wk≍k−βw_{k}\asymp k^{-\beta} with β>1\beta>1, and a width-dd network effectively computes the top Feff​(d)≍dαF_{\mathrm{eff}}(d)\asymp d^{\alpha} features. Then the residual loss satisfies L⁡(d)−L∞≍d−α⁡(β−1)L(d)-L_{\infty}\asymp d^{-\alpha(\beta-1)}, giving scaling-law exponent η=α⁡(β−1)\eta=\alpha(\beta-1). Moving from α=3/2\alpha=3/2 to α=2\alpha=2 multiplies η\eta by 4/34/3—testable by estimating β\beta from SAE importance distributions and manipulating reset quality in toy models. This prediction connects to [11], who show that the strong-superposition regime produces robust power-law scaling.

Prediction A.2 (Correlation-adjusted interface; [Conjectured]).

Define an effective coherence weighted by co-activation:

μeff2:=max⁡∑j≠ii⁡Πi​j​⟨ϕi,ϕj⟩2,\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}:=\max_{i}\sum_{j\neq i}\Pi_{ij}\,\langle\phi_{i},\phi_{j}\rangle^{2},

where Πi​j\Pi_{ij} is the co-activation probability. Under an average-case version of the interface compatibility inequality, F≲d1/2/μeff2F\lesssim d^{1/2}/\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2}. If correlations reduce μeff\mu_{\mathrm{eff}} below d−1/2d^{-1/2}, the effective capacity exponent rises above 3/23/2, formalizing the intuition of [13] that constructive interference relaxes worst-case bounds.

Remark A.3.

Prediction A.2 is heuristic: the bound F≲d1/2/μeff2F\lesssim d^{1/2}/\mu_{\mathrm{eff}}^{2} does not follow directly from the published interface inequality and requires a new average-case theorem replacing the worst-case s​μs\mu term of Theorem 14. We include it as a conjecture to guide future work.

Appendix B Proof Details: Interface Compatibility Inequality

With εcomp​(d)=C1​s/d\varepsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}(d)=C_{1}s/\sqrt{d} and εcorr,max​(d,F)=C2​d1/4/(F1/2​s1/4)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr,max}}(d,F)=C_{2}d^{1/4}/(F^{1/2}s^{1/4}), the template compatibility condition is εcomp≤εcorr,max\varepsilon_{\mathrm{comp}}\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{corr,max}}:

C1​sd≤C2​d1/4F1/2​s1/4.C_{1}\frac{s}{\sqrt{d}}\leq C_{2}\,\frac{d^{1/4}}{F^{1/2}s^{1/4}}.

Rearranging gives

F≤(C2/C1)2d3/2s−5/2.F\leq(C_{2}/C_{1})^{2}\,d^{3/2}\,s^{-5/2}.

For s=O⁡(1)s=O(1) this is F=O⁡(d3/2)F=O(d^{3/2}).

Appendix C Nuclear Norm Inequality Details

For any M∈ℝF×FM\in\mathbb{R}^{F\times F} with SVD M=∑k=1rσk​uk​vk⊤M=\sum_{k=1}^{r}\sigma_{k}u_{k}v_{k}^{\top}:

|tr⁡(M)|=|∑kσk​uk⊤​vk|≤∑kσk​|uk⊤​vk|≤∑kσk=‖M‖∗.|\mathrm{tr}(M)|=\Big|\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}\,u_{k}^{\top}v_{k}\Big|\leq\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}\,|u_{k}^{\top}v_{k}|\leq\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}=\left\lVert M\right\rVert_{*}.

By Cauchy–Schwarz on the rr-vector (σ1,…,σr)(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}): ‖M‖∗2≤r​∑kσk2=r​‖M‖F2\left\lVert M\right\rVert_{*}^{2}\leq r\sum_{k}\sigma_{k}^{2}=r\,\left\lVert M\right\rVert_{F}^{2}. With r≤dr\leq d: |tr⁡(M)|2≤d​‖M‖F2|\mathrm{tr}(M)|^{2}\leq d\,\left\lVert M\right\rVert_{F}^{2}.

An alternative route uses eigenvalues:

|tr⁡(M)|2=|∑λk|2≤(∑|λk|)2≤r​∑|λk|2≤r​∑σk2|\mathrm{tr}(M)|^{2}=\Big|\sum\lambda_{k}\Big|^{2}\leq\Big(\sum|\lambda_{k}|\Big)^{2}\leq r\sum|\lambda_{k}|^{2}\leq r\sum\sigma_{k}^{2}

by Schur’s inequality. Both paths yield the same result.

Appendix D Experimental Data

This paper does not report new experiments. The empirical observations in Section 12 are drawn entirely from the companion study [2], which trained TopK Sparse Autoencoders (k=64k=64, expansion ratio dSAE=8​dd_{\mathrm{SAE}}=8d) on residual-stream activations of three language models at six sparsity levels with 3–5 random seeds each. Table 2 reports the baseline metrics (sparsity 0) included for reproducibility of the motivational SAE context; these measurements are not used in any proof.
